chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Upper Limb > Forearm
keyPoints: The deep fascia of the forearm (antebrachial fascia) is thicker posteriorly than anteriorly and gives partial origin to the forearm muscles both in front and behind.

It is strengthened above by the bicipital aponeurosis; along the posterior border of the ulna it forms a strong ulnar aponeurosis giving origin to flexor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus; and at the wrist it thickens into the flexor retinaculum in front and the extensor retinaculum behind.
The cubital fossa is an inverted triangular hollow in front of the elbow joint occupying the upper one third of the front of the forearm.

Its base is directed upwards as an imaginary line between the two epicondyles of the humerus; the lateral boundary is brachioradialis, the medial boundary pronator teres, and the apex the meeting of brachioradialis overlapping pronator teres.
The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by brachialis medially and supinator laterally.

The roof is skin and superficial fascia containing parts of the cephalic and basilic veins and the median cubital vein connecting them, the anterior branches of the lateral and medial cutaneous nerves of the forearm, and the supratrochlear lymph nodes in its upper lateral part, plus deep fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis.

Contents of the cubital fossa from medial to lateral: the median nerve (which leaves by passing between the two heads of pronator teres), the termination of the brachial artery with the beginning of ulnar and radial arteries, the tendon of biceps, and the radial nerve with the beginning of its posterior interosseous branch.
The bicipital aponeurosis lies in the roof and separates the median cubital vein superficially from the median nerve and terminal brachial artery deep to it.
The muscles of the front of the forearm are the flexors of wrist and digits and the pronators, arranged in superficial and deep groups.

The superficial group is five muscles arising by a common tendon from the anterior surface of the medial epicondyle (common flexor origin): four superficial - pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris from lateral to medial - and one deep, flexor digitorum superficialis.

The superficial group is supplied by the median nerve except flexor carpi ulnaris, which is supplied by the ulnar nerve; their common actions are flexion of the wrist (except pronator teres) and weak flexion of the elbow.

Pronator teres has a humeral head from the common flexor origin and an ulnar head from the coronoid process, inserts into the pronator tuberosity in the middle of the lateral surface of the radial shaft, and gives powerful pronation of the forearm and weak elbow flexion.

Flexor carpi radialis inserts into the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals and flexes and abducts the hand at the wrist; flexor carpi ulnaris has humeral and ulnar heads, inserts into the pisiform then the 5th metacarpal and hamate, and flexes and adducts the hand; palmaris longus inserts into the apex of the palmar aponeurosis, flexing the wrist and tensing the aponeurosis.

Flexor digitorum superficialis has a humero-ulnar head from the common flexor origin and coronoid process and a radial head from the anterior oblique line of the radius, inserting by four tendons each splitting into two slips into the sides of the middle phalanges of the medial four fingers.
The median nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres, while the ulnar nerve passes between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.

The deep group of the front is three muscles: flexor pollicis longus laterally and flexor digitorum profundus medially superficially, and pronator quadratus deepest, running horizontally in front of the lower parts of radius and ulna.
The deep group is supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve except the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, which is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Flexor digitorum profundus arises from the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna and the adjacent interosseous membrane and inserts into the distal phalanges of the medial four fingers, its tendons passing deep to those of flexor digitorum superficialis.
The muscles of the back of the forearm are the extensors of wrist and digits; all their tendons except brachioradialis pass deep to the extensor retinaculum.

The superficial extensor group is seven muscles from lateral to medial: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris and anconeus, arising from a common extensor origin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the lateral epicondyle except brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and anconeus.

Brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and anconeus are supplied by the radial nerve itself; extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi and extensor carpi ulnaris are supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

The extensor expansion is a strong triangular fibrous sheet with its base proximal and apex distal covering the dorsum of the proximal phalanx of each medial four fingers, receiving the extensor tendons of the digits and the tendons of lumbricals and interossei.

At the proximal interphalangeal joint the extensor expansion divides into an intermediate part attached to the base of the middle phalanx and two collateral parts attached to the base of the terminal phalanx.

The deep extensor group is five muscles from above downwards: supinator, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis, all supplied by the posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve.

Supinator surrounds the upper third of the shaft of the radius, arising from the supinator crest and fossa of the ulna and from the lateral epicondyle, lateral collateral ligament of the elbow and annular ligament, inserting into the posterior, lateral and anterior aspects of the upper third of the radius above the oblique lines; it supinates the forearm.
The supinator is pierced by the posterior interosseous nerve, which curves round the upper part of the radius inside the muscle substance, splitting it into superficial and deep layers.

The anatomical snuffbox is a triangular hollow at the lateral part of the dorsum of the wrist, clearly visible when the thumb is extended, bounded medially by the tendon of extensor pollicis longus and laterally by the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

Its roof is skin, superficial fascia containing the beginning of the cephalic vein and digital branches of the superficial radial nerve, and deep fascia; its floor is the styloid process of the radius, the scaphoid proximally and the trapezium distally.
The snuffbox contains the radial artery as it crosses the dorsum of the hand, whose pulsations can be felt there, and the tendons of extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis cross its floor.

The ulnar nerve arises in the axilla from the medial cord; it descends on the medial side of the third part of the axillary artery and the medial side of the upper half of the brachial artery, then at the middle of the arm pierces the medial intermuscular septum into the posterior compartment.

At the elbow the ulnar nerve descends behind the medial epicondyle grooving it, enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and descends on flexor digitorum profundus covered by that muscle in the upper two-thirds; in the lower third it becomes superficial between the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris medially and the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis laterally.

At the wrist the ulnar nerve descends superficial to the flexor retinaculum, lateral to the pisiform and medial to the ulnar artery, ending in front of the retinaculum by dividing into a superficial (mainly cutaneous) and a deep (mainly muscular) branch.

The ulnar nerve gives no branches in the axilla and arm; in the forearm it gives articular branches to the elbow joint, muscular branches to flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, a palmar cutaneous branch to the skin of the medial third of the palm, and a dorsal cutaneous branch dividing into two dorsal digital nerves for the medial third of the dorsum of the hand and the medial one and a half fingers.

The median nerve arises in the axilla by two roots from the medial and lateral cords forming the median nerve trunk on the lateral side of the axillary artery; it descends lateral to the third part of the axillary artery and the upper half of the brachial artery, crosses the brachial artery opposite the insertion of coracobrachialis and descends medial to its lower half lying on brachialis.

In the cubital fossa the median nerve lies on brachialis deep to the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the median cubital vein; it leaves by passing between the two heads of pronator teres, separated posteriorly by the deep head from the ulnar artery.

It then reaches the deep surface of flexor digitorum superficialis and descends between it and flexor digitorum profundus, becoming superficial immediately above the wrist between the tendon of flexor carpi radialis laterally and the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis medially, and enters the palm deep to the flexor retinaculum, ending in the carpal tunnel by dividing into lateral and medial terminal divisions.

The median nerve gives no branches in the axilla and arm; in the forearm it gives articular branches to the elbow and superior radio-ulnar joints, muscular branches to pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis, the anterior interosseous nerve, and a palmar cutaneous branch.

The anterior interosseous nerve arises as the median nerve emerges between the heads of pronator teres, descends on the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane between flexor pollicis longus laterally and flexor digitorum profundus medially, disappears deep to pronator quadratus and supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus plus the inferior radio-ulnar and wrist joints.

The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises about one inch above the wrist and descends superficial to the flexor retinaculum to supply the skin of the lateral two-thirds of the palm, except a proximal small part of thenar skin supplied by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

The superficial radial nerve begins in front of the lateral epicondyle as the continuation of the radial nerve immediately below the origin of the posterior interosseous nerve and descends in the lateral part of the front of the forearm overlapped by brachioradialis, lateral to the radial artery.

It is separated from the radial artery by a triangular gap in the upper third, lies closely lateral to it in the middle third, and in the lower third leaves it by turning backwards round the lateral surface of the radius under cover of the brachioradialis tendon; short of the wrist it pierces the deep fascia and crosses the roof of the anatomical snuffbox to the dorsum of the hand.

It ends by dividing into five dorsal digital nerves - two for both sides of the thumb, one for the lateral border of the index and two for the clefts between index, middle and ring fingers - supplying the dorsal aspect of the lateral three and a half fingers as far as their distal halves and the skin of the lateral two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand.

The posterior interosseous nerve arises from the radial nerve in front of the lateral epicondyle, descends under cover of brachioradialis, supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis and supinator then pierces supinator, emerging on the back of the forearm to descend with the posterior interosseous artery between the superficial and deep extensors.

It then passes under cover of extensor pollicis longus to join the anterior interosseous artery on the back of the interosseous membrane and descends with it deep to the extensor retinaculum through the 4th compartment to the back of the wrist, ending in an expanded termination (pseudoganglion) giving articular filaments.

The posterior interosseous nerve supplies the inferior radio-ulnar, wrist and some intercarpal joints, and all extensor muscles of the back of the forearm, superficial and deep, except brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and anconeus.
The flexor retinaculum is a thickened transverse band of deep fascia crossing in front of the carpus, converting the anterior concavity of the bony carpal arch into the carpal tunnel.

It attaches medially to the pisiform and hook of hamate; laterally it splits into a superficial lamina attached to the tubercle of the scaphoid and crest of the trapezium and a deep lamina attached to the medial lip of the groove on the trapezium, the two laminae forming with that groove a special tunnel for the tendon of flexor carpi radialis and its synovial sheath.
Below, the flexor retinaculum is continuous with the deep fascia of the palm especially the apex of the palmar aponeurosis; above, with the deep fascia on the front of the forearm.

Structures passing superficial to the flexor retinaculum from medial to lateral: ulnar nerve, ulnar artery, palmar cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve, tendon of palmaris longus and palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.

Structures deep to it, in the carpal tunnel: nine tendons (four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and one of flexor pollicis longus), two synovial sheaths (ulnar and radial bursae), the median nerve lying directly under cover of the retinaculum, and the recurrent branch of the deep palmar arch as the deepest structure; the tendon of flexor carpi radialis with its sheath runs in the special tunnel.
Muscles attached to the anterior surface of the flexor retinaculum: thenar muscles laterally and hypothenar muscles medially by origin, and the tendon of palmaris longus in the middle by insertion.
The carpal tunnel has sides and floor formed by the anterior surface of the carpal bones forming the bony carpal arch, and a roof formed by the flexor retinaculum.

The extensor retinaculum is a thickened band of deep fascia extending obliquely across the back of the wrist, attached laterally to the lower end of the radius and medially to the triquetral and pisiform; fibrous septa to ridges on the back of the lower end of the radius divide the space deep to it into six compartments.

Extensor retinaculum compartments from lateral to medial: 1st holds abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; 2nd extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis; 3rd extensor pollicis longus; 4th the four tendons of extensor digitorum, extensor indicis, the posterior interosseous nerve and the anterior interosseous artery; 5th extensor digiti minimi; 6th extensor carpi ulnaris.

The radial artery begins in the cubital fossa below the elbow joint at the level of the neck of the radius as the smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery, passes downwards and laterally in the lateral part of the front of the forearm, is overlapped above by brachioradialis and becomes superficial below where its pulsation is felt between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis medially and brachioradialis laterally.
At the wrist the radial artery winds backwards round the lateral side of the wrist through the anatomical snuffbox to the dorsum of the hand.

Radial artery branches: the radial recurrent artery ascending in front of the lateral epicondyle to anastomose with the radial collateral artery; muscular branches to the radial side muscles; the anterior carpal artery joining the anterior carpal arch; and the superficial palmar artery which descends through and supplies the thenar muscles and completes the superficial palmar arch with the terminal ulnar artery.

The ulnar artery begins in the cubital fossa below the elbow joint as the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, runs obliquely downwards and medially in the upper third then vertically along the medial side of the front of the forearm.

At the wrist the ulnar artery descends superficial to the flexor retinaculum lateral to the ulnar nerve and the pisiform and medial to the hook of hamate, ending in the hand as the superficial palmar arch.

Ulnar artery branches near the elbow: the anterior ulnar recurrent artery ascending in front of the medial epicondyle to anastomose with the anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral; the posterior ulnar recurrent artery ascending between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris to the back of the medial epicondyle to meet the superior ulnar collateral; and the common interosseous artery.

The common interosseous artery is a short trunk arising about one inch below the beginning of the ulnar artery which descends backwards to the upper margin of the interosseous membrane and divides into anterior and posterior interosseous arteries.

The anterior interosseous artery, the larger, descends on the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous nerve, pierces the membrane at the upper border of pronator quadratus to reach the back of the forearm and anastomose with the termination of the posterior interosseous artery, then descends with the posterior interosseous nerve deep to the extensor retinaculum in the 4th compartment to join the posterior carpal arch.

Its branches are the median artery which accompanies and supplies the median nerve (vasa nervosa), muscular branches, nutrient arteries of both radius and ulna, and a descending branch deep to pronator quadratus joining the anterior carpal arch.

The posterior interosseous artery, smaller, passes backwards above the interosseous membrane and descends between the superficial and deep muscles of the back of the forearm with the posterior interosseous nerve, becoming small and ending by anastomosing with the anterior interosseous artery; near its origin it gives the posterior interosseous recurrent artery to the back of the lateral epicondyle plus muscular branches.

In the forearm the ulnar artery gives muscular branches to the ulnar side muscles; at the wrist it gives the anterior carpal artery which forms the anterior carpal arch with its radial counterpart, and the posterior carpal artery which forms the posterior carpal arch.

Book gives the surface anatomy of the radial artery as a line from a point midway between the two epicondyles medial to the biceps tendon to a point at the front of the lower end of the radius where the pulsation is felt, continued round the radial side of the wrist to the proximal end of the first metacarpal interosseous space.

Book gives the surface anatomy of the ulnar artery as a line through three points: midway between the epicondyles medial to the biceps tendon; the medial side of the forearm at the junction of the upper third with the lower two-thirds; and just lateral to the pisiform at the wrist.

keyPoints: The deep fascia of the palm has three parts: a thin lateral part over the thenar eminence, a thin medial part over the hypothenar eminence, and a thick strong central part over the intermediate compartment called the palmar aponeurosis.

The palmar aponeurosis is the thickest and strongest part of the palmar deep fascia, firmly attached to the overlying palmar skin by dense fibrous tissue, and it protects the tendons, vessels and nerves going to the fingers.

It is triangular: its apex is directed upwards, fuses with the flexor retinaculum and receives the insertion of the palmaris longus tendon; its base divides into four slips, each passing to the root of a finger and becoming continuous with the fibrous flexor sheath of one of the medial four fingers.

Its lateral margin is continuous with the much thinner deep fascia over the thenar eminence; its medial margin is continuous with that over the hypothenar eminence and gives origin to palmaris brevis.

The palmar aponeurosis sends three palmar septa deeply: the lateral palmar septum to the 1st metacarpal, pierced by the branches of the median nerve to the thenar muscles; the medial palmar septum to the 5th metacarpal, pierced by the deep branches of the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery; and the intermediate palmar septum passing from near the lateral margin between the index tendons and the other finger tendons to the palmar surface of the 3rd metacarpal.

The fascial spaces of the hand (intermediate compartment of the palm) are bounded ventrally by the palmar aponeurosis, dorsally by the 3rd, 4th and 5th metacarpals with the related interossei and adductor pollicis, medially by the medial palmar septum and laterally by the lateral palmar septum.

The mid-palmar space is the medial space, bounded laterally by the intermediate palmar septum and medially by the medial palmar septum; it contains the long flexor tendons to the 3rd, 4th and 5th fingers, the 2nd, 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the digital nerves and vessels to the medial three and a half fingers.

The thenar space is the lateral space, bounded laterally by the lateral palmar septum, medially by the intermediate palmar septum and dorsally by the transverse head of adductor pollicis and its covering fascia; it contains the long flexor tendons of the index and thumb, the 1st lumbrical, and the digital nerves and vessels to the lateral one and a half fingers.
Both spaces communicate distally with the finger webs and proximally with the space deep to the common synovial sheath in the carpal tunnel.

The space of Parona lies between pronator quadratus posteriorly and the flexor tendons of the forearm in front and is continuous with the deep palmar space behind the long flexor tendons in the carpal tunnel.

The superficial distal pulp space of the finger is the pulp space of the distal phalanx at the fingertip, very tightly packed with small lobules of subcutaneous fat separated by many fibrous septa passing from the skin to the periosteum of the distal phalanx.

The thenar muscles - abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis - arise from the crest of the trapezium and the lateral side of the flexor retinaculum, insert into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (opponens into the lateral surface of the shaft of the first metacarpal), and are supplied by the recurrent muscular branch of the median nerve.

Adductor pollicis arises by an oblique head from the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals and a transverse head from the front of the shaft of the 3rd metacarpal, inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb in common with flexor pollicis brevis, is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and adducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint.

The hypothenar muscles - abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi - arise from the pisiform, hook of hamate and medial side of the flexor retinaculum, insert into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger (opponens into the medial surface of the shaft of the 5th metacarpal), and are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

Palmaris brevis lies in the superficial fascia of the palm beneath the skin of the hypothenar eminence, arises from the flexor retinaculum and medial border of the palmar aponeurosis, inserts into the skin of the medial side of the palm, is supplied by the superficial branch of the ulnar nerve and deepens the hollow of the palm by wrinkling and raising that skin.

The lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus in the palm; the lateral two each arise by a single head from the lateral margin of the lateral two tendons, and the medial two each by two heads from the adjacent margins of the medial three tendons.

Lumbrical tendons turn backwards on the lateral side of the metacarpophalangeal joints of the medial four fingers to join the corresponding extensor expansions and are finally inserted into the dorsal aspects of the bases of the distal phalanges.

The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; acting with the interossei they flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints, putting the fingers into the writing position.

Palmar interossei arise by a single head from the palmar surfaces of the metacarpals of the thumb, index, ring and little fingers; the 1st inserts into the medial side of the thumb's proximal phalanx and the others into the extensor expansions; they adduct the fingers towards the middle finger (mnemonic PAD).

Dorsal interossei arise by two heads from the adjacent sides of the metacarpals and insert into the extensor expansions - laterally for the index and middle, medially for the middle and ring; they abduct the fingers away from the middle finger (mnemonic DAB).

All interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; the middle finger has two dorsal interossei and the first dorsal interosseous is the largest, while the first palmar interosseous is often absent. The middle finger is the reference line for abduction and adduction.

The common flexor sheath (ulnar bursa) encloses the eight tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus in the carpal tunnel, with a parietal layer lining the tunnel and a visceral layer covering the tendons; it extends proximally above the flexor retinaculum and distally ends at the middle of the metacarpals but continues with the little finger's sheath.

The flexor pollicis sheath (radial bursa) encloses the tendon of flexor pollicis longus, extends proximally and continues distally to the tendon's insertion, and usually communicates with the ulnar bursa in the carpal tunnel.

Digital synovial sheaths (digital bursae) enclose the flexor tendons in each finger in two layers, extending proximally to the distal palm crease - except the little finger, which connects with the ulnar bursa - and distally to the tendon insertions.

The flexor carpi radialis tendon has its own synovial sheath in its own compartment in the groove of the trapezium; the two layers of any synovial sheath are separated by a very narrow space with minimal synovial fluid.
The synovial sheaths of the index, middle and ring fingers do not communicate with the ulnar bursa but are separated from it by a short distance where the tendons are bare.

The ulnar nerve enters the palm in front of the medial part of the flexor retinaculum, lateral to the pisiform and just medial to the ulnar artery, and divides there into superficial and deep terminal branches.

The superficial branch of the ulnar nerve descends deep to palmaris brevis, supplying it, then divides into two palmar digital branches supplying the skin on the palmar surfaces of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.

The deep branch of the ulnar nerve dips between abductor and flexor digiti minimi with the deep branch of the ulnar artery, pierces opponens digiti minimi, curves round the hook of hamate and turns laterally across the palm in the concavity of the deep palmar arch, ending near the lateral border of the palm.

The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, the medial two lumbricals, all eight interossei, adductor pollicis, sometimes an additional supply to flexor pollicis brevis, and gives articular branches to the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints.
The median nerve enters the palm deep to the flexor retinaculum in the carpal tunnel and divides into a smaller lateral and a medial division.

The lateral division gives the recurrent branch to the thenar muscles - flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis - then divides into three palmar digital branches: two for both sides of the thumb and one for the lateral side of the index which also supplies the 1st lumbrical.

The medial division divides into two branches: one to the cleft between index and middle fingers giving a muscular branch to the 2nd lumbrical and two palmar digital branches, and one to the cleft between middle and ring fingers dividing into two palmar digital branches.

The palmar digital branches of the median nerve supply not only the whole palmar aspect but also turn backwards to supply the distal half of the dorsal aspects of the lateral three and a half fingers.
The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except five - the lateral two lumbricals and the three thenar muscles - which are supplied by the median nerve.

The ulnar artery enters the palm superficial to the medial part of the flexor retinaculum, lateral to the ulnar nerve and pisiform and covered by palmaris brevis, and divides in front of the retinaculum into deep and superficial divisions.

Its deep division passes backwards between abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis, penetrates opponens digiti minimi and anastomoses with the end of the deep palmar arch at the base of the 5th metacarpal, accompanied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; the superficial division curves laterally across the palm as the superficial palmar arch.

The superficial palmar arch lies immediately deep to the palmar aponeurosis but superficial to the flexor tendons and the digital branches of the median nerve, crossing the palm at the level of the midshaft of the metacarpals, distal to the deep palmar arch; it is formed mainly by the ulnar artery and completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery at the thenar eminence.

The superficial palmar arch gives four palmar digital arteries: one to the medial side of the little finger from its medial end under cover of palmaris brevis, and three common palmar digital arteries from its convexity to the three clefts between the medial four fingers, each joined by the corresponding palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch and dividing into a pair of proper palmar digital arteries.

The radial artery leaves the forearm by winding backwards round the lateral side of the wrist superficial to the lateral ligament, crosses the anatomical snuffbox deep to abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis and over the tendons of extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (where its pulsation can be felt), and leaves deep to the tendon of extensor pollicis longus.

On the dorsum of the hand it descends to the proximal part of the 1st interosseous space and passes forwards between the two heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous into the palm, emerging between the oblique and transverse heads of adductor pollicis and running medially immediately distal to the bases of the metacarpals as the deep palmar arch.

Radial artery branches on the dorsum of the hand: the posterior carpal artery which forms the posterior carpal arch with its ulnar counterpart, the first dorsal digital branch to the lateral border of the thumb, and the first dorsal metacarpal artery which divides into two dorsal digital branches for the adjacent sides of thumb and index.

Radial artery branches in the palm: the princeps pollicis artery arising as the artery emerges between the two heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous and dividing at the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb into the two palmar digital branches of the thumb; the radialis indicis artery of variable origin running along the lateral side of the index on the palmar aspect; and the deep palmar arch.

The deep palmar arch lies deep to the flexor tendons, crossing the palm immediately distal to the bases of the metacarpals, proximal to the superficial palmar arch; it is formed mainly by the radial artery and completed by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery at the base of the 5th metacarpal, and is concave towards the wrist with the deep branch of the ulnar nerve in its concavity.

The deep palmar arch gives three palmar metacarpal arteries to the clefts between the medial four fingers joining the common digital branches of the superficial arch, three perforating branches passing dorsally through the proximal parts of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th intermetacarpal spaces to join the dorsal metacarpal arteries, and recurrent branches ascending in front of the wrist joint to the anterior carpal arch.
There are four arterial arches in the hand: anterior carpal, posterior carpal, superficial palmar and deep palmar.

The anterior carpal arch lies on the front of the carpus deep to the flexor tendons and is formed by the anterior carpal branches of ulnar and radial arteries, a descending branch from the anterior interosseous artery and recurrent branches from the deep palmar arch, together forming a cruciate anastomosis.

The posterior carpal arch lies on the back of the carpus deep to the extensor tendons, formed by the posterior carpal branches of ulnar and radial arteries and the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries; it gives the 2nd, 3rd and 4th dorsal metacarpal arteries, each bifurcating into two dorsal digital branches for the adjacent sides of the medial four fingers, plus a dorsal digital branch to the medial border of the little finger. The 1st dorsal metacarpal artery arises from the radial artery on the dorsum of the hand.

appliedNotes: Book states: when the superficial distal pulp space is inflamed it is very painful because pus is entrapped under tension in the narrow space and compresses the nerves.

Book states: the blood vessels of the shaft and head, but not the base, of the terminal phalanx traverse the pulp space, so severe infection may cause thrombosis of those vessels and death of the shaft and head of the distal phalanx while the base is spared.

Book states: infection of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th synovial sheaths remains localised to their fingers, but infection of the thumb or little finger (radial and ulnar bursae) may spread to the palm, carpal tunnel and forearm.
Book states infection may extend from the space of Parona to the spaces of the palm and vice versa.

Book gives the surface anatomy of the superficial palmar arch as a curved line with its convexity distal, drawn across the hand from the distal border of the root of the extended thumb; and of the deep palmar arch as a curved line 4 cm long from a point just distal to the hook of hamate at the level of the proximal border of the fully extended thumb.

The chapter ILO asks the student to 'Define the fibrous flexor sheathes and describe its attachment', but the chapter has no dedicated section on the fibrous flexor sheaths - they are mentioned only in passing where the palmar aponeurosis slips become continuous with them.

keyPoints: The veins of the upper limb are divided into superficial and deep groups which communicate freely and are provided with valves.
Superficial veins run in the superficial fascia; the book states they are larger and more important than the deep veins, into which they finally end, and they begin in the dorsum of the hand.
The superficial dorsal venous network (arch) is a network of veins in the superficial fascia on the dorsum of the hand receiving the dorsal digital and metacarpal veins.

The cephalic vein begins from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch just behind the styloid process of the radius, runs upwards onto the anterior surface of the forearm ascending on its lateral side, crosses the lateral part of the roof of the cubital fossa, runs in a groove along the lateral side of the arm and reaches the deltopectoral groove.
Just below the clavicle the cephalic vein pierces the deep fascia and clavipectoral fascia to end in the terminal part of the axillary vein.

The basilic vein begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, ascends along the medial surface of the forearm, turns to the anterior surface just below the elbow, crosses the medial part of the roof of the cubital fossa, pierces the deep fascia at the middle of the arm at the insertion of coracobrachialis and ascends medial to the brachial artery.
At the lower border of teres major the basilic vein is joined by the two venae comitantes of the brachial artery, together forming the axillary vein.

The median vein of the forearm begins near the wrist by union of a few veins from the palm, ascends in the middle of the front of the forearm and below the elbow ends in the basilic or cephalic vein, or divides into a median basilic vein joining the basilic and a median cephalic vein joining the cephalic.

The median cubital vein connects the cephalic and basilic veins in the superficial fascia of the roof of the cubital fossa, crossing superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve; the book states it is the most prominent superficial vein in the body and is used for intravenous injection.

The deep veins are the venae comitantes, two accompanying each main artery and anastomosing with each other, with those of the radial and ulnar arteries joining those of the brachial artery, plus the axillary vein.

Deep lymph nodes of the upper limb are the five groups of axillary lymph nodes plus a few nodes in the cubital fossa at the bifurcation of the brachial artery, in the arm along the brachial artery and in the forearm along the radial and ulnar arteries.
Superficial lymph nodes are few scattered nodes in two groups: supratrochlear (epitrochlear) and infraclavicular (deltopectoral).

Supratrochlear nodes lie in the superficial fascia of the roof of the cubital fossa above the medial epicondyle along the basilic vein; they receive afferents from the medial side of the hand and forearm and send efferents to the lateral group of axillary lymph nodes.

Infraclavicular nodes lie along the cephalic vein in the deltopectoral groove immediately below the clavicle; they receive few lymphatics accompanying that vein and send efferents to the apical group of axillary lymph nodes.

Superficial lymph vessels on the medial side of the wrist follow the basilic vein in the forearm, pierce the deep fascia with it and end in the lateral group of axillary nodes, some ending just above the elbow in the supratrochlear nodes.

Superficial lymph vessels on the lateral side of the wrist follow the cephalic vein; at the insertion of deltoid most incline medially to pierce the deep fascia and end in the lateral (humeral) group of axillary nodes, while a few continue with the cephalic vein to the apical group.

Deep lymph vessels follow the main arteries - radial, ulnar and brachial - and end in the lateral group of axillary lymph nodes; deep vessels from the scapular region end in the subscapular group and those from the pectoral region in the pectoral group.

chapters.bookTitle: CUTANEOUS NERVE SUPPLY OF THE UPPER LIMB and NERVE INJURIES (Chapter 9)
keyPoints: Cutaneous supply of the posterior side of the shoulder, axilla and upper arm is by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm from the radial nerve in the axilla, supplying the back of the arm from the deltoid tuberosity to the elbow.

The medial side is supplied by the intercostobrachial nerve (lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve) over the axillary floor and upper half of the medial arm, and the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm from the medial cord over the lower half of the medial arm.

The lateral side is supplied by the lateral supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4) over the upper half of deltoid, the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm from the posterior branch of the axillary nerve over the lower half of deltoid, and the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm from the radial nerve in the spiral groove over the lateral arm from the deltoid tuberosity to the elbow.

The forearm is supplied by the lateral cutaneous nerve (from the musculocutaneous) laterally front and back, the medial cutaneous nerve (from the medial cord) medially front and back, and the posterior cutaneous nerve (from the radial) over the middle posterior forearm.
In the palm the ulnar nerve supplies the medial third and the median nerve the lateral two-thirds, except the ball of the thumb which is supplied by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
On the palmar surface of the fingers the ulnar supplies the medial one and a half and the median the lateral three and a half fingers plus their distal dorsal halves.

On the dorsum the ulnar supplies the medial third and the radial the lateral two-thirds; on the dorsal fingers the ulnar supplies the medial one and a half and the radial the lateral three and a half but only their proximal halves, the distal halves being supplied by the median.

The book notes that branches of the median nerve overlap the whole area of skin supplied by the superficial radial nerve except a triangular area on the dorsum of the web between thumb and index, which is supplied only by the superficial radial nerve.

Upper trunk injury (Duchenne-Erb's paralysis) may result from excessive displacement of the head to one side with depression of the shoulder on the other, causing excessive traction or tearing of the C5,6 roots; the book notes this may occur in infants during delivery as a birth injury.

Erb's paralysis produces the 'porter's tip deformity': the shoulder is adducted from paralysis of deltoid and supraspinatus and medially rotated from paralysis of infraspinatus and teres minor, the elbow is extended from paralysis of biceps and most of brachialis, and the forearm is pronated from paralysis of biceps; sensation is lost on the lateral side of the upper limb.

Lower trunk injury (Klumpke's paralysis) may result from excessive abduction of the arm with traction or tearing of the C8 and T1 roots - as in falling from a height clutching an object, or traction of an infant's arm during delivery - and also from a cervical rib or malignant lower deep cervical lymph nodes.

Because C8 and T1 fibres are mainly distributed through the ulnar nerve to the lumbricals and interossei, Klumpke's paralysis gives a claw hand with hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints from the unopposed extensor digitorum and flexion of the interphalangeal joints from the unopposed flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus loss of abduction and adduction of the fingers; sensation is lost on the medial side of arm and forearm, the medial third of the palm and the medial one and a half fingers.

Axillary nerve injury is frequent in dislocation of the shoulder joint, fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus and pressure of a badly adjusted crutch in the armpit; it gives impaired shoulder abduction and a flat shoulder from deltoid wasting, with a patch of sensory loss over the lower half of the deltoid.
Long thoracic nerve injury may occur during radical mastectomy and gives winging of the scapula, difficulty in protraction of the shoulder girdle and difficulty in raising the arm above the head.

Ulnar nerve injury may occur posterior to the medial epicondyle from fracture, dislocation or compression at the elbow; in the cubital tunnel formed by the tendinous arch connecting the humeral and ulnar heads of flexor carpi ulnaris; or at the wrist from cut or stab wounds.

Ulnar injury at the wrist gives partial claw hand - extension of the metacarpophalangeal joints of the 4th and 5th fingers with flexion of their interphalangeal joints from paralysis of their lumbricals and interossei, the 2nd and 3rd fingers being less affected because their lumbricals are median-supplied.

Ulnar injury at the wrist also gives loss of abduction and adduction of the fingers so the patient cannot grip paper placed between the fingers, loss of adduction of the thumb from paralysis of adductor pollicis so paper cannot be gripped between thumb and index, flattening of the hypothenar eminence and hollowing between the metacarpals on the dorsum.

Ulnar injury above or at the elbow makes the clawing less apparent in the 4th and 5th fingers because the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus is also paralysed, and adds radial deviation of the hand from paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris; sensory loss then covers the medial third of the palm, the medial one and a half fingers front and back, and the medial third of the back of the hand.

Median nerve injury above the elbow may follow supracondylar fracture of the humerus; pronator syndrome is entrapment near the elbow between the two heads of pronator teres from trauma, muscular hypertrophy or fibrous bands; at the wrist it may follow cut or stab wounds or carpal tunnel syndrome.

Median injury at the wrist gives the ape (monkey's) hand deformity: wasting of the thenar muscles with flattening of the thenar eminence, loss of opposition of the thumb, lateral rotation of the thumb so the 1st metacarpal becomes parallel to the others from loss of opponens tone, and adduction of the thumb because adductor pollicis is intact while the abductor is paralysed.

Sensory loss in median injury at the wrist covers the lateral three and a half fingers palmar and distal dorsal aspects; if the palmar cutaneous branch is included, also the lateral two-thirds of the palm; in carpal tunnel syndrome there is paraesthesia just over the lateral three and a half fingers.

Median injury above the elbow adds to the ape hand: loss of pronation from paralysis of both pronators, ulnar deviation from paralysis of flexor carpi radialis, weak flexion of the wrist from paralysis of most of its flexors, loss of flexion of the index and middle phalanges (pointing fingers - these fingers remain straight when making a fist) from paralysis of flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus, and loss of flexion of all joints of the thumb from paralysis of flexor pollicis longus and brevis.

Radial nerve injury may follow fracture of the shaft of the humerus in the spiral groove, pressure of a badly adjusted crutch in the armpit, or a drunkard falling asleep with one arm over the back of a chair (Saturday night palsy); the posterior interosseous nerve may be injured in fracture of the head, neck or upper shaft of the radius or downward dislocation of the radial head.

Radial nerve injury above the elbow gives wrist drop and finger drop from paralysis of all extensors of wrist and fingers, which is very disabling because a firm grip is impossible while the wrist is flexed; it also impairs extension of the elbow against resistance from triceps affection and causes failure of supination of the extended forearm.
In posterior interosseous nerve injury there is only finger drop without wrist drop, because the intact extensor carpi radialis longus alone can maintain extension of the wrist.

Radial sensory effects vary with the level of injury: a patch of sensory loss over the lower half of deltoid; a small area of complete sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand between the 1st and 2nd metacarpals, restricted because of overlap by adjacent nerves; and paraesthesia over the posterior surface of arm and forearm, the lower lateral side of the arm, the lateral two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand and the posterior surfaces of the proximal phalanges of the lateral three and a half fingers.

keyPoints: The acromio-clavicular joint is a synovial joint of the plane variety between the acromial end of the clavicle and the medial margin of the acromion; it usually contains an articular disc dividing its cavity into two incomplete compartments, and its capsule is strengthened above by the acromio-clavicular ligament.

The acromio-clavicular joint shares a little in the movements of the shoulder girdle and in transmitting forces from the upper limb to the clavicle, but the main medium transmitting those forces is the coraco-clavicular ligament.

The coraco-clavicular ligament is a very strong bond connecting the clavicle with the coracoid process, in two incompletely separated parts: a quadrilateral trapezoid part forming the anterolateral portion, attached below to the upper surface of the coracoid process and above to the trapezoid line on the lower surface of the lateral third of the clavicle; and a conoid part forming the posteromedial portion, a dense band attached below to the upper and posterior aspect of the bend of the coracoid process and above to the conoid tubercle of the clavicle.

The coraco-clavicular ligament limits the movements of the acromio-clavicular joint, prevents dislocation of the acromial end of the clavicle, and is the main medium by which the scapula and the upper limb are suspended from the clavicle.
The sterno-clavicular joint is a synovial modified saddle joint between the clavicular notch of the manubrium sterni with the first costal cartilage and the sternal end of the clavicle.

Its intra-articular disc is a flat circular fibrocartilaginous disc attached by its circumference to the fibrous capsule, dividing the joint into two separate cavities; it absorbs the forces transmitted from the shoulder region through the clavicle and prevents dislocation of the sternal end of the clavicle.
The capsule of the sterno-clavicular joint surrounds it completely, thicker in front and behind and thin above and below.

Its ligaments are the anterior and posterior sterno-clavicular ligaments, the interclavicular ligament passing from the upper aspect of one clavicle's sternal end to the other across and attached to the upper margin of the manubrium, and the costo-clavicular ligament.

The costo-clavicular ligament is attached below to the upper aspect of the 1st costo-chondral junction and above to the margins of the impression on the lower surface of the medial end of the clavicle; it prevents excessive elevation and protraction of the clavicle, the same function as subclavius which acts as a dynamic ligament.
The sterno-clavicular joint is stable, its strength depending on its ligaments and the intra-articular disc.

Movements of the shoulder girdle occur at both the acromio-clavicular and sterno-clavicular joints; the scapula moves on the clavicle at the acromio-clavicular joint but movement there is limited, while movement at the sterno-clavicular joint increases the range of scapular movement.
Shoulder girdle elevation is by the upper fibres of trapezius, levator scapulae and both rhomboids; depression by pectoralis minor and the inferior fibres of trapezius.
Upward rotation (glenoid cavity facing upwards) is by the upper and lower fibres of trapezius with serratus anterior; downward rotation by levator scapulae and both rhomboids.
Protraction is by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor; retraction by the middle fibres of trapezius and both rhomboids.
The shoulder joint is a synovial polyaxial (ball and socket) joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity deepened by the labrum glenoidale.

The labrum glenoidale is a fibrocartilaginous rim whose base is fixed to the circumference of the glenoid cavity; it deepens and widens the articular socket and protects the edges of the glenoid cavity.

The fibrous capsule is attached medially to the circumference of the glenoid cavity beyond the labrum, extending above onto the root of the coracoid process to include the supraglenoid tubercle inside the capsule; laterally to the anatomical neck of the humerus except below, where it descends onto the medial side of the surgical neck.

The capsule has two to three perforations: an anterior one through which the synovial membrane communicates with the subscapular bursa, an antero-lateral one for the tendon of the long head of biceps, and an inconstant posterior one which may communicate with the bursa deep to the infraspinatus tendon.

The synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule and is reflected over the intracapsular non-articular bony parts, is continuous with the subscapular bursa through the anterior perforation, and envelops the tendon of the long head of biceps as a tubular sheath emerging through the lateral perforation.

Intracapsular structures of the shoulder joint: the tendon of the long head of biceps, the head of the humerus and the medial part of its surgical neck, the labrum glenoidale, the glenoid cavity with the supraglenoid tubercle, and the synovial membrane.

Shoulder joint ligaments: three weak gleno-humeral ligaments strengthening the anterior capsule from the anterior margin of the glenoid cavity to the lesser tuberosity and anatomical neck; the stronger coraco-humeral ligament strengthening the upper capsule from the coracoid process to the upper border of the greater tuberosity; the transverse humeral ligament, a broad band from lesser to greater tuberosity converting the intertubercular groove into a canal and acting as a retinaculum for the long head of biceps; and the coraco-acromial ligament.

Bursae related to the shoulder joint: the subscapular bursa deep to subscapularis between it and the front of the capsule; a bursa deep to the infraspinatus tendon behind the capsule; the subacromial bursa between deltoid and the capsule, prolonged under the acromion separating it from the supraspinatus tendon and not communicating with the joint cavity; a bursa between the coracoid process and the capsule; and a subcutaneous bursa on the upper surface of the acromion.

The shoulder joint is weak, unstable and easily dislocated because the fitting of its bony parts is poor - a very large humeral head against a small shallow glenoid cavity - because the capsule and its ligaments are weak and lax, and because the capsule is not directly supported by any muscle from below.

The joint is supported above by the tendons of supraspinatus and the long head of biceps, in front by subscapularis and behind by infraspinatus and teres minor; the tendons of supraspinatus, subscapularis, infraspinatus and teres minor form the rotator muscle cuff which reinforces the capsule and provides active support during movement, while deltoid covers the joint in front, behind and laterally.

Below, the joint has no muscular support: the capsule is lax and forms a fold bulging downwards into the upper part of the axilla, directly related to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, and stretched when the arm is fully abducted; the long head of triceps supports the capsule from below only when the arm is abducted.

The joint is protected from above by the coraco-acromial arch: the strong flat triangular coraco-acromial ligament, with its apex attached to the tip of the acromion and its base to the lateral margin of the upper surface of the coracoid process, together with the two processes forms an arch immediately above the joint acting as a secondary socket for the humeral head.

Shoulder flexion is by the clavicular head of pectoralis major, the anterior fibres of deltoid and coracobrachialis, assisted by the long head of biceps; extension by the posterior fibres of deltoid, teres major and latissimus dorsi, with the sternocostal head of pectoralis major extending the flexed arm.

Shoulder abduction is by supraspinatus and the middle (acromial) fibres of deltoid; adduction by pectoralis major, teres major, latissimus dorsi, coracobrachialis, subscapularis, infraspinatus and teres minor.

Medial rotation is by pectoralis major, teres major, latissimus dorsi, the anterior fibres of deltoid and subscapularis; lateral rotation by infraspinatus, the posterior fibres of deltoid and teres minor; circumduction is a combination of all these.

Mechanism of abduction: supraspinatus initiates abduction through the first small range, the middle (acromial) fibres of deltoid continue it to about a right angle, after which the head cannot move further because the greater tuberosity impinges on the coraco-acromial ligament; raising the arm above the head is then achieved by the scapula rotating over the chest wall so the glenoid cavity faces upwards, done by the upper and lower fibres of trapezius with the lower five digitations of serratus anterior.

The book states that during abduction of the arm there are simultaneous movements of the shoulder joint and shoulder girdle in a fixed ratio, continuing until the whole remaining movement takes place by upward rotation of the scapula.

The elbow joint is a synovial uniaxial (hinge) joint; proximally the condyle of the humerus (trochlea and capitulum), distally the trochlear notch of the ulna and the head of the radius, the trochlea articulating with the trochlear notch and the capitulum with the upper circular surface of the radial head.

The elbow capsule is attached above and in front to the humerus just above the coronoid and radial fossae extending to the roots of the epicondyles, above and behind just above the olecranon fossa, and below to the margins of the olecranon and the annular ligament encircling the radial head.
The elbow and the superior radio-ulnar joint have a common capsule; the capsule is thin in front and behind but thick on each side because of the strong collateral ligaments.

The medial (ulnar) collateral ligament is fan-shaped, attached above to the medial epicondyle and below to the medial margin of the trochlear notch, and prevents abduction of the elbow; the lateral (radial) collateral ligament is a strong triangular ligament attached by its apex to the lateral epicondyle and by its base to the outer surface of the annular ligament, and prevents adduction.
Elbow extension is by triceps assisted by anconeus; flexion mainly by brachialis and biceps, assisted by brachioradialis and the superficial flexors of the forearm.

The superior radio-ulnar joint is a synovial uniaxial (pivot) joint in which the circumference of the head of the radius rotates against the radial notch of the ulna; its capsule is continuous above with that of the elbow joint and their joint spaces are continuous, and its synovial membrane is a downward prolongation of the elbow's.

The annular ligament is attached to the anterior and posterior borders of the radial notch of the ulna and encircles the head of the radius; it is slightly narrower below than above, which prevents the head of the radius from being dislocated downwards.

The quadrate ligament is a quadrangular band connecting the lower margin of the radial notch of the ulna to the medial aspect of the neck of the radius, lying just below the joint and closing its cavity from below.
The inferior radio-ulnar joint is a synovial uniaxial (pivot) joint between the head of the ulna, the ulnar notch of the radius and the articular disc.

The articular disc is a fibrocartilaginous triangular disc attached by its apex into a depression between the styloid process and the inferior surface of the ulnar head; it separates the cavity of the inferior radio-ulnar joint from that of the wrist joint.

The capsule of the inferior radio-ulnar joint is slightly thickened anteriorly and posteriorly and lax above to allow the wide movement of pronation; its synovial membrane projects upwards as a small pouch, the recessus sacciformis, between radius and ulna in front of the interosseous membrane.

Pronation and supination occur at the superior and inferior radio-ulnar joints around a vertical axis passing from the centre of the head of the radius above to the rough impression of the head of the ulna below, at the attachment of the apex of the articular disc.

Mechanism: the head of the radius rotates within the ring formed by the radial notch and the annular ligament; the shaft of the radius swings while the shaft of the ulna stays relatively fixed; at the inferior joint the lower end of the radius and the articular disc rotate around the head of the ulna, carrying the hand, in a circle centred on the attachment of the apex of the disc to the root of the ulnar styloid process.
In supination the radius and ulna lie parallel, the palm faces forwards, the thumb is directed laterally and the interosseous membrane is tense.

In pronation the shaft of the radius lies across the front of the shaft of the ulna so its lower end lies medial to the ulna, the hand moves with the radius so the palm looks backwards, the thumb is directed medially, the interosseous membrane becomes lax and the carrying angle at the elbow disappears.

Supinators are biceps - the main supinator of the flexed elbow - and supinator, plus brachioradialis which puts the forearm in the midprone position; pronators are pronator teres and pronator quadratus, plus brachioradialis in the same midprone role.

The book states supinators are in general more powerful than pronators, that biceps is the most powerful supinator during elbow flexion, and that supinator is the main supinator during elbow extension.

The interosseous membrane joins radius and ulna, attached laterally to the interosseous border of the radius, medially to that of the ulna, ending above at a free border below the radial tuberosity and blending below with the capsule of the inferior radio-ulnar joint; its fibres run obliquely downwards and medially from radius to ulna.

The interosseous membrane increases the area, front and back, for the origin of forearm muscles - flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus from its anterior surface, and abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis and extensor indicis from its posterior surface - and, by the direction of its fibres, transmits forces received by the radius from the hand upwards to the humerus.

The wrist joint is a synovial biaxial (ellipsoid) joint; its proximal articular surface has an ellipsoid outline slightly concave in both directions, formed by the inferior surface of the lower end of the radius - a lateral triangular part for the scaphoid and a medial quadrilateral part for the lunate - and the articular disc of the inferior radio-ulnar joint below the head of the ulna.

The distal articular surface is formed by the scaphoid, lunate and triquetral from lateral to medial, together forming an oval surface convex in all directions; the scaphoid and lunate lie below the radius and the triquetral below the articular disc.
The ulna does not come into direct contact with the carpal bones and does not share in the wrist joint because of the articular disc, so the wrist joint is called the radio-carpal joint.

Wrist ligaments: the radial collateral ligament from the tip of the radial styloid to the lateral side of scaphoid and trapezium; the ulnar collateral ligament from the end of the ulnar styloid to the medial side of triquetral and pisiform; the palmar radiocarpal ligament running obliquely and medially from the anterior margin of the lower end of the radius and its styloid to the anterior surface of scaphoid, lunate and triquetral; the palmar ulnocarpal ligament from the base of the ulnar styloid and the anterior margin of the disc to the anterior surface of lunate and triquetral; and the dorsal radiocarpal ligament running downwards and medially to the dorsal surfaces of the same three bones, weaker than the palmar one.

Wrist flexion is by flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus and flexor pollicis longus; extension by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digitorum, extensor indicis and extensor digiti minimi.

Wrist adduction is by flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris; abduction by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, flexor carpi radialis, abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

Relations of the wrist joint: anteriorly the flexor retinaculum and the structures passing both deep and superficial to it; posteriorly the extensor retinaculum and the structures deep to it; postero-laterally the anatomical snuffbox.

The mid-carpal joint is a synovial modified ellipsoid joint between the proximal row of carpal bones as one unit and the distal row as the second, with a common capsule and common joint cavity; the carpal bones are held together by strong interosseous ligaments and its movements are complementary to those of the wrist but much more limited.

The carpo-metacarpal joint of the thumb is a synovial biaxial saddle joint between the superior surface of the trapezium and the base of the 1st metacarpal, each articular surface being concavo-convex.

It is relatively freely mobile because the 1st metacarpal lies at a right angle to the plane of the palm and the fibrous capsule is loose; flexion and extension occur parallel to the palm, abduction and adduction at right angles to the palm, and opposition is flexion plus medial rotation.

The carpo-metacarpal joints of the medial four fingers are synovial plane joints with minimal gliding movement; the little finger has an opponens muscle which can move its metacarpal forwards and laterally towards the thumb, helping to cup the hand.

The metacarpo-phalangeal joints are synovial ellipsoid joints between the convex heads of the metacarpals and the shallow concavities of the bases of the proximal phalanges; that of the thumb is classified as hinge because abduction and adduction are restricted there.

At the metacarpo-phalangeal joints of the medial four fingers, flexion is by lumbricals, interossei and flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus; extension by extensor digitorum, extensor indicis and extensor digiti minimi; adduction by the palmar interossei; abduction by the dorsal interossei.

The book states abduction and adduction at the metacarpo-phalangeal joints are free when the fingers are extended but become gradually limited as the fingers flex, becoming impossible when the hand is completely closed.

At the metacarpo-phalangeal joint of the thumb, flexion is by flexor pollicis longus and brevis and extension by extensor pollicis longus and brevis, with abduction and adduction very much restricted.

The interphalangeal joints are synovial uniaxial (hinge) joints allowing flexion and extension only; in the medial four fingers flexion is by flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis (the latter acting only on the proximal interphalangeal joint), and extension by lumbricals, interossei, extensor digitorum, extensor indicis and extensor digiti minimi; in the thumb flexion is by flexor pollicis longus and extension by extensor pollicis longus.

definitions.text: Very strong bond connecting the clavicle with the coracoid process of the scapula, in trapezoid and conoid parts; the main medium by which the scapula and upper limb are suspended from the clavicle.
Ligament from the 1st costo-chondral junction to the lower surface of the medial end of the clavicle, preventing excessive elevation and protraction of the clavicle.
Fibrocartilaginous rim fixed to the circumference of the glenoid cavity, deepening and widening the articular socket and protecting its edges.
The tendons of supraspinatus, subscapularis, infraspinatus and teres minor, intimately related to the fibrous capsule, reinforcing it and providing active support during movement.
The coraco-acromial ligament with the coracoid and acromion processes, forming a secondary socket immediately above the shoulder joint supporting the head of the humerus from above.
Bursa between deltoid and the capsule of the shoulder joint, prolonged under the acromion separating it from the supraspinatus tendon; it does not communicate with the joint cavity.

Ligament attached to the anterior and posterior borders of the radial notch of the ulna encircling the head of the radius, narrower below than above so preventing downward dislocation of the radial head.
Quadrangular band connecting the lower margin of the radial notch of the ulna to the medial aspect of the neck of the radius, closing the joint cavity from below.
Small upward pouch of the synovial membrane of the inferior radio-ulnar joint between radius and ulna in front of the interosseous membrane.
Alternative name for the wrist joint, so called because the ulna does not share in its formation.
Synovial modified ellipsoid joint between the proximal and distal rows of carpal bones, each acting as one unit.

Book states the lax inferior fold of the shoulder joint capsule bulges into the upper axilla directly related to the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and is stretched when the arm is fully abducted - the anatomical basis of the axillary nerve injury in shoulder dislocation described in Chapter 9.
Book states abduction of the arm is arrested at the glenohumeral joint because the greater tuberosity impinges on the coraco-acromial ligament, after which further elevation is scapular rotation.

EXAM SCOPE: the department's orientation sheet declares the joints of the hand outside the examinable syllabus. Within this chapter that covers the mid-carpal joint, the carpo-metacarpal joints (thumb and medial four fingers), the metacarpo-phalangeal joints and the interphalangeal joints (physical pages 288-291). The shoulder girdle joints, shoulder joint, elbow joint, radio-ulnar joints, interosseous membrane and wrist joint on pages 270-287 remain in scope.

The chapter ILO promises interpretation of clinical problems from dislocation of each joint in relation to important nerves or arteries, but the only such note in the chapter text is the clavicle-fracture remark; the shoulder dislocation / axillary nerve link is made in the nerve injuries chapter instead.
